claims.text: Molecular dynamics using an EAM or modified-EAM potential combined with free-energy sampling can be used to study the size-dependent thermal response of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Smaller FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles will have lower melting or phase-transition onset temperatures than larger nanoparticles.
The FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles are synthesized with an equiatomic or near-equiatomic distribution in a nanocrystalline solid-solution state.
A specially parameterized EAM potential can represent the multicomponent interactions needed for the proposed FeCuCrCoNi simulations.
Temperature ramps or isothermal holds can be simulated over a range of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticle sizes.
Vacuum or inert-atmosphere conditions isolate atomic-scale thermal phenomena in these simulations.
Particle size determines the surface-to-volume ratio of a nanoparticle.
The size-dependent surface-to-volume ratio modifies atomic diffusion and phase stability in FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles.
Smaller nanoparticles contain a higher fraction of surface atoms.
A higher fraction of surface atoms enhances atomic mobility and surface diffusion, facilitating earlier melting or phase transitions.
EAM-based molecular dynamics can reveal temperature-driven structural and chemical evolution in multicomponent alloy nanoparticles.
The precise results depend on the accuracy of the multicomponent EAM parameterization.
The exact temperature shift and extent of structural evolution depend on the selected free-energy sampling method.
Experimental validation is needed to establish the quantitative accuracy of the simulation predictions.
A controlled comparison of FeCuCrCoNi nanoparticles between 5 and 20 nm can test whether transition onset temperature decreases with particle size.
Failure to observe a statistically significant decrease in melting or transformation onset temperature with decreasing size would falsify the hypothesis.
